20762:
I'd like to respond to Adam's inquiry relating to upgrading low-res near full screen images to a hi-res display. Attached below is Adam's inquiry.

Actually, I also have an inquiry relating to the higher level software that allows one to generate a low-res image, such that it can be displayed on the Astrocade console or emulator.

I have a lot of experience programming graphics for the Astrocade using machine language (ML). I would be considered a "low-level" programmer having this expertise. A step upward from ML would be to program using assembly language (AL), for example, using the Zmac assembler. Both of these languages allow a programmer to display (write) full screen images using a minimal amount of program bytes.

Here is my inquiry.

It looks like there is higher level software that may be easier to use than ML or AL but apparently has a "downside" in that there is extra processing bytes that must be attached along with the low-res display image, so the image can be displayed on say, the Astrocade console or emulator.

Could someone spend some time to enlighten me as to what specific software was utilized to generate the low-res images collected by Chris plus provide the compatibility to display the images on the Astrocade's low-res screen map? A fundamental description of the software would be very much appreciated by MCM Design. Thanks.

I would also like to explain what I mean that ML or AL allows one to minimize the amount of bytes required to display a full or near full image on the Astrocade.

The Nutting Manual, which is archived on the Bally Alley, provides a good system description of both the low and hi-res modes along with related output/input ports. Unfortunately, the custom address/data chips on the Astrocade motherboard are wired only for low-res.

Looking at the low-res screen map, the TV display is 40 bytes across by 102 byte lines high. Screen RAM utilizes 40 x 102 = 4080 bytes (0FF0H). Each byte defines 4 pixels. Each pixel color is defined by 2 bits providing the possibility of 1 out of 4 colors (colors 00, 01,10 and 11).

There is also an additional 16 RAM bytes that are not part of screen RAM. So, the 4080 + 16 bytes gives you 4096 bytes (4KB) of RAM.

The 4KB of RAM is the ONLY RAM on the motherboard. So, errand RAM bytes in the form of variables, vector blocks, program flags and the Z80 stack must be located at the bottom of screen RAM and hidden from view by the vertical blanking line.

Note that when displaying static graphics, even large screen images, errand RAM bytes are normally not required. So it is possible to display a screen image on all 102 lines of screen RAM. This is what I would call a "write only" option because the Z80 CPU only writes graphics to screen RAM. It does not read any stack area, variables, etc. in screen RAM because these errand bytes are normally not necessary for a write only graphic display.

Now let's say the screen image is only going to be 100 lines high. That would require 40 x 100 = 4000 bytes of RAM. That would leave you with 2 lines x 40 + 16 = 96 bytes to work with any program errand bytes, if you wanted it to.

I'm going to call these 4000 bytes the raw data block image (RDBI). This is the byte count to display a 4 color, static graphic image in screen RAM using 100 line bytes.

The Z80 CPU has a very powerful data block transfer (move) instruction called a LDIR (opcode ED B0). This instruction can copy huge amounts of data from a data block (source) in ROM to a destination (location) in screen RAM.

The three 16 bit Z80 registers BC, DE and HL must be set up with the desired parameters prior to the execution of the LDIR instruction, where:

HL = ROM (source) starting address
DE = screen RAM (destination) starting address = 4000H
BC = number of bytes to copy = 4000D = 0FA0H

What am I saying? The total Z80 machine code byte count for the BC, DE, HL and LDIR instructions would be 3 + 3 + 3+ 2 = 11 instruction bytes.

That is, it would take just 11 Z80 machine code bytes to copy a 4000 byte RDBI from an Astrocade game cartridge to the TV display (screen RAM). The copy would execute at a blazing speed.

It just so happens that the Astrocade on-board ROM includes a UPI sub #94 called Move, which is really a LDIR instruction. Use sub #94 and you can reduce the 11 instruction byte count down to 8 bytes with a slightly reduced copy execution speed. Wow!

A few extra bytes in the game cartridge would be required to jump to the program, set up 4 screen parameters and end the program with a Z80 Halt instruction.

There's more.
With just a few more bytes, you could select the RDBI from the Astrocade menu.
By using the magic expand option and settling for a 2 color screen image, you could cut down the 4000 byte RDBI to 2000 bytes.
Using the magic expand option would allow you to program an 8KB game cartridge with 3 two color 100 line screen images.

What about the possibility of upgrading (increasing the image detail) a low-res screen image to hi-res?

Since it is not clear to me at this time how Chris' collection of images were initially created, I can only make a few comments.

The upgrade would likely be a challenge. Hi-res maps 80 bytes per line and low-res 40 bytes per line. Perhaps some compatibility software could be created.

Could an 8KB game cartridge display a hi-res screen image? In a way, yes it could.
For example, since you would have around 8000 bytes of cartridge ROM to work with, you could create a 4 color hi-res screen image 80 bytes wide by 100 lines high. The image could be centered on the hi-res display having a single color "framing" around the image's perimeter.

As an option, a 2 color magic expanded image could be increased larger than the 80 x 100 area or you could program a pair of 2 color 4000 bytes screen RAM images using the 80 x 100 area.

20804:
I find it hard to believe, but a full year has passed since my 2022 Bally
contribution toward the Vintage Computing Christmas Challenge. At the 11th
hour before the deadline completely escaped me, I felt inspired to
contribute to the 2023 challenge. Again I opted to pursue the "wild"
category to exercise much more creative freedom than the strict depiction
expected in the main challenge. I always enjoy adding additional elements of
snow/winter to these themes and find Bally's graphic capabilities, however
limited, to be helpful in that regard. The snowflake demonstration last year
received a fair deal of praise and more importantly introduced people to the
Bally itself, since many including the event organizer had not heard of the
system prior to that.

 

Challenge Description:
https://logiker.com/Vintage-Computing-Christmas-Challenge-2023

 

My Entry Demonstration (mostly via emulation for clarity, but a brief demo
on hardware too): https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j6eZmLUV180
<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j6eZmLUV180&feature=youtu.be> 

 

ZIP File: Attached (WAV file can be played through emulation or ordinary
device as usual).

 

2022 Entry Discussion: https://groups.io/g/ballyalley/topic/95933071/

 

Most who participate in these challenges adhere to more traditional
approaches, using ASCII text output. As this group understands Bally/Astro
BASIC has one of the largest sized fonts out there, so when the challenge
calls for 18-20+ lines of text in one view and we can only squeeze about 11
in (and manually plotting characters via XY, CX or CY also has the issue of
overwriting one glyph data with another if they overlap at all). The
alternative is to have fun with the line and/or box commands. Blue RAM BASIC
can fit 16 lines, so still out of the league for this to display perfectly.

 

To achieve this output I first drew a square window to establish the general
boundaries where the required pattern would populate in a ping-pong sort of
fashion. I then statically decorated the outer frame with what vaguely
resembles some drifting snow and snowfall in a slightly procedural manner.
From there the program displays the output in three phases. First the drawn
stars/snowflakes alternate in a way to resemble a partially developed
snowflake pattern. Then each of them fills completely to match the intended
pattern. Finally, they will endlessly loop through various stages of
appearance to give off a more scattered "snowing out the window" style
effect. But all while retaining the original pattern of the challenge.

 

This entire entry went from idea to full implementation just over these
evening hours before the deadline. I had other ideas I briefly experimented
with but ran out of time, including one that would populate the snowflakes
randomly into the pattern instead of in the pong style it does. In the end
I'm still satisfied with the output, but the code is not unoptimized
compared to last year since my only focus was to get something developed.
Time permitting next year I feel Bally could still put up a fighting chance
in the main challenge. Since its main commands are tokenized there are a lot
of bytes able to be saved compared to many BASIC variants. And it is also
easy to verify the total number of bytes used by checking SZ after loading
the code and comparing that to the original 1800.

 

I had hoped this month to get the group a couple of my experimental Bally
programs circulated for use. But they are still works in progress on my own
dev box. Will see what I can manage with them this week but odds are it'll
be in the coming months when I have any of my internal Bally tools packaged
up for outside use. 

 

Thank you, Merry Christmas and Happy Holidays! 

 

Matt

On December 26, 2023, Adam wrote, "Scroll Mode of 4 will pause automatically
when the screen is full."

 

Great tip, I was unaware of this scroll mode control option! I see it is
clearly documented on page 31 of the Astro BASIC manual including for this
particular use case. I often had a need to review certain lines of code
(which can be accessed directly with LIST 100 to start at line 100, for
instance) but didn't realize there was a way to stop it at the end of each
page. Somewhat embarrassing that I overlooked this feature considering I
have had the manual open so often. This BASIC implementation continues to
impress me for its small footprint but capable features, even this scroll
mode functionality is omitted from many BASICs I've used.

 

Excerpting from the manual to reiterate the various scroll mode options, for
future reference:

 

SCROLL MODE CONTROL

 

The two-letter SCROLL MODE variable is SM, which can be set to any one of
five values:

 

SM=0 - Scrolls conventionally.

 

SM=1 - Suppresses scrolling. Cursor stays at bottom.

 

SM=2 - Holds cursor at screen bottom, clears after each carriage return.

 

SM=3 - Clears the screen and resets cursor to screen top.

 

SM=4 - AUTO-PAUSE. Allows listing to fill the screen to the bottom line, at
which time the computer will go into the pause mode until you touch any key.
Then the screen will clear and start printing from the top line down,
automatically pausing again when the screen is full. This is the ideal mode
for viewing your program listings "one page at a time."

The Astrocade console is terribly designed to dissipate internally generated heat.
To reduce the risk and help protect your Astrocade from failure, I highly recommend the following:

Never, never operate your Astrocade with the console top in place.

To help dissipate motherboard generated heat, remove the horizontal metal shielding that covers the top of the motherboard.
Note that the RF modulator is grounded only by the motherboard bottom shielding via a long, narrow flexible copper contact. Inspect and clean the contact point, removing any aged tarnish.

The 40 pin custom data chip typically has a cheap, flat aluminum heat sink glued on top of it.
Ideally, you want this chip to run cool to warm, NOT "very hot" to the touch.
See the static discharge warning below before touch testing the chip or its heat sink to determine if it's running hot.
The data chip may not have any internal thermal protection.
I have observed that when the chip is heating up abnormally (too hot), graphic issues may occur and likely lead to a graphic crash.
Never attempt to pry off this cheap heat sink to replace it with a better 40 pin finned heat sink.
A pry off attempt may crack the chip's fragile plastic packaging.
Instead, install a finned heat sink on top of the cheap heat sink.
You don't have to glue on the finned heat sink. Regular heat sink compound smeared onto the bottom of the heat sink will eventually become tacky enough to keep the finned sink from sliding off the cheap sink.

Use forced air to help protect the custom data chip from overheating.
Buy a 6 inch fan (at True Value Hardware?) and run it at low speed.
Note the power supply heat sinks are elevated, but the custom data chip heat sinking is low-profile and is in the midst of physical obstructions.
Placement of the fan is important.
You want to direct as much of the moving air as possible to actually strike the custom data chip.
Moving air that strikes obstructions will likely redirect the airflow, possibly reducing the flow toward the data chip.
The best placement of the fan may be behind the motherboard power switch.
The second choice would be in the vicinity near the left rear corner of the Astrocade console.
Neither of my modified for hi-res Astrocades utilize a RF modulator, which can block air flowing from left to right.
So, the second choice works great for me.

Always remove the black Bally power transformer in a wall outlet after you are finished using your Astrocade because the transformer will still power +5V circuitry even with the motherboard power switch in the "off " position.
Don't believe me? Check out how the power switch is connected on the motherboard electronic schematic.
Optionally, plug the transformer into a power strip and leave the motherboard power switch "on". Use the power strip to completely turn on/off your Astrocade.

Cut down an 120vac extension cord and splice into it a fast blow "in-line" fuse holder.
Size the fuse as low as possible (1A or less?) to help protect the Bally transformer from overheating/burnout due to a short or near short that occurs within the motherboard.

Replace the old larger power supply electrolytic capacitors.
If needed, contact Allen Schweitzer, who may be able to schedule a recap for you for a fee.

STATIC DISCHARGE WARNING
Never touch motherboard components with your shoes on.
This sounds silly, but this precaution can reduce the risk of a static discharge.
Optionally, if you have a metal light fixture near your Astrocade, touch the metal first to discharge any bodily static charge before touching a component.

What is the risk of a static discharge if you just touch the Astrocade console in any way with your shoes on?
I live in a semi-arid climate. When I plan to handle an Astrocade or electronic components, I will remove my shoes.
I can testify that I have experienced a static discharge only a few times within a time span of many years. I am a very active Astrocade user.

Anyone else want to add to this list of recommendations?

By the way, if you have the expertise, consider building an audio/composite video drivers board to replace the RF modulator. This is a major Astrocade upgrade.
Reference the posted doc "MCM Design Hi-Res News - Report 6", Nov 2022, message #19665.

I am 90% confident that we can make images like the above on the Bally.   They are 160x100 images using only 4 colors of the Bally Palette per line.  (There are some weird artifacts that I can't completely explain but this is how the algorithm is working at the moment - I have ideas how to make it better.)  We have 8K of ROM space so plenty for the image data.  Here is how it will work.  We'll LDIR the image data to the screen using the proper 0 through 3 values.  Then we'll enter a loop.  Ideally there is a vertical refresh port or register and a horizontal port or refresh.  If not, then I will have to count cycles and interrupts usually get in the way of that.   In the Nuttig Manual I can see:

EH         Vertical Line Feedback

FH         Horizontal Address Feedback

I can't figure out exactly what these are but I know they are HORAF, and VERAF.  I can't find anything in the Nuttig manual about what feedback they provide or how.  What I am used to is a simple BIT that tells when we are in the horizontal blank and same for vertical blank to figure out where the end of a line draw is and an end of a screen draw.  This seems much more sophisticated.  Anybody know how they work?  Anyway, we'll wait for the horizontal refresh to start and during that refresh we'll change the color registers to the stored values, the loop will wait again and repeat the process.  When we get to the bottom of the screen we will start all over again.

The color data will take up 100 lines * 4 bytes for colors = 400 bytes for color data.  If we figure this one out, then the next step is to go 8 colors per line and change the horizontal split position for each line as well.  I'm not sure how to optimize that but I am pretty sure it can be done in a way that isn't excessively slow.  First things first is to figure out how HORAF and VERAF work.

The OR instruction is the critical element because of how JP NZ treats the zero flag.

Here's a more detailed breakdown:

* 

DEC (HL) : Decrements the value at the memory location pointed to by the HL register. This is your loop counter.

* 

LD A, (HL) : Loads the decremented value of the counter into the accumulator A.

* 

OR A : Performs a bitwise OR on the accumulator. This operation is primarily used here to set the Zero flag if the accumulator (which holds the decremented counter value) is zero.

* 

SBC HL, HL : Sets HL to zero, but more importantly, this instruction affects the flags based on the result. Since the result is zero, the Zero flag will be set due to this operation.

* 

JP NZ, REDO : This instruction checks if the Zero flag is not set (NZ - Not Zero) and jumps if the condition is true. The important flag for this decision is the one set by the OR A instruction, not SBC HL, HL.

In this sequence, the OR A instruction is crucial. It sets the Zero flag based on whether the counter has reached zero. If the counter (decremented by DEC (HL) ) is not zero, the OR A instruction will not set the Zero flag, and the JP NZ, REDO will cause the program to loop back to REDO. If the counter is zero, OR A sets the Zero flag, and the JP NZ, REDO instruction will not jump, breaking the loop.

LD A, (HL): Loads the decremented value of the counter into the accumulator A.

   -    
OR A: Performs a bitwise OR on the accumulator. This operation is primarily used here to set the Zero flag if the accumulator (which holds the decremented counter value) is zero.

   -    
SBC HL, HL: Sets HL to zero, but more importantly, this instruction affects the flags based on the result. Since the result is zero, the Zero flag will be set due to this operation.

   -    
JP NZ, REDO: This instruction checks if the Zero flag is not set (NZ - Not Zero) and jumps if the condition is true. The important flag for this decision is the one set by the OR A instruction, not SBC HL, HL.


In this sequence, the OR A instruction is crucial. It sets the Zero flag based on whether the counter has reached zero. If the counter (decremented by DEC (HL)) is not zero, the OR A instruction will not set the Zero flag, and the JP NZ, REDO will cause the program to loop back to REDO. If the counter is zero, OR A sets the Zero flag, and the JP NZ, REDO instruction will not jump, breaking the loop.

20921:
The main things that would cause the symptoms you describe are C6, possibly C1 and any custom chip. To do an immediate check on the customs without removing them is to check for excessive heat. The DATA chip will be quite hot but the other ones should be warm at best. to check the capacitors, you'll need to lift the positive lead and see if any of the voltages come back. DO NOT DO THIS FOR ANY LENGTH OF TIME. You we be adding more stress. The positive leads are the ones closest to you when you are putting in a cartridge. make sure that the wire from the diode is going to this side. The next step would be to quickly pass your hand over the components on the board. The large heat sink on the regulator will be hot, as will the heat sink on the 10V regulator. The 15v (or maybe you have the 12V unit) regulator should be relatively cool. I have found even the tiniest of parts can get very hot if they are bad.The best way to check the customs is to remove them all. then if the voltages come up, replace them one at a time. MAKE SURE YOU DON"T GET THEM MIXED UP!!! They have their power pins in different spots. If left on in the wrong socket, it can fry that chip fairly quickly.
If these tests don't get any of the 3 voltages back, there is a serious problem with some component. There is a short somewhere.

If the pots are flat bottomed, you're better off using Deoxit, or at the very least, a fast drying non-silicone electronic contact cleaner.  Make sure to get one that does NOT EAT PLASTIC.  I have suggestions on that if you'd like.For the "bell" bottomed pots, I clean the resistor plate (and fingers) with actone first, then Everclear (to remove any residue) then Goo Gone, leaving just a bit of "film" on there from that.  Then I put 2 of the tiniest dabs (1 of each) of white lithium grease and di-electric grease on the resistor plate.  Too much of either and they will jitter.  It doesn't take much of either.On the flat bottomed ones, if they are stiff, just keep pumping the cleaner to the pot and twisting.  It may be the old grease on the shaft, but 4 out of 5 times (or more) just dumping the spray in the pot will eventually loosen them up.I'm flattered to have my work on display!!!

20984:
> Maybe there is a way to do this from the MAME emulator now?  Is that possible?

If the WAV files can be loaded into MAME, then you can use the MAME debugger to save raw .BIN data.  For example, you can use a command line like:

mame -debug astrocde astrobas -nofilter -keepaspect -window

to start MAME with AstroBasic in debugger mode.  Debug mode is halted by default, so press F5 or select Debug/Run from the menu to run the debugger.  You can then load the program as you normally would.  Once the .WAV file is loaded, you can issue a save command in the debugger window.  For example:

save "C:\mypath\filename.bin", 4000,1000

will save 4 kilobytes of raw data starting at hex address 4000.

I also started work on a tool that sends commands to the MAME debugger with virtual keystrokes, and will save raw buffers and/or BASIC source code in txt2prg format.  Maybe that could be useful?
